questions.q: Define imagery and list the five senses it engages. Give one example of each type from daily life (not from the text).
questions.a: Imagery is descriptive language that appeals to the five senses: visual (sight – e.g., "crimson sunset"), auditory (sound – e.g., "train whistle"), olfactory (smell – e.g., "wet earth after rain"), gustatory (taste – e.g., "bitter gourd"), tactile (touch – e.g., "rough bark"). A wrong answer listing only "visual description" or confusing imagery with "imagination" reveals a fundamental gap: the student will miss how Lakhia uses smell/touch to convey grief (e.g., "still air", "clutched stomach") and thus cannot analyze the essay's sensory architecture.

questions.q: In the sentence "I was enveloped by a great mist of protection and I wanted to emerge from that mist and discover myself," identify the metaphor, name its tenor and vehicle, and explain two qualities of the vehicle that map onto the tenor.
questions.a: Metaphor: "mist of protection". Tenor: childhood experience of parental overprotection. Vehicle: mist/fog. Mapped qualities: (1) Obscures vision → parents' decisions blocked her view of life's realities; (2) Dampens sound/isolates → she was cut off from normal peer interactions (e.g., didn't know boys' behaviour). A wrong answer calling this a "simile because it has 'like' implied" or identifying only "protection" as the comparison shows inability to unpack metaphor's implicit, multi-layered transfer of qualities.

questions.q: Locate the temple paragraph ("Another argument I often had with my grandmother..."). Underline all sensory words and classify each by sense (V/A/O/G/T). Then explain why the author includes olfactory and tactile details but omits gustatory imagery in this specific paragraph.
questions.a: Sensory words: "grandeur of the architecture" (V), "feel the curve of the stones" (T), "scent of incense, flowers and sandalwood" (O), "hear the ringing of the bells" (A), "taste the panchamrut" (G), "palms and soles... touch different surfaces" (T). Gustatory *is* present ("taste the panchamrut") – a trick question testing careful reading. The author includes all five senses to enact "sensitivity" (full sensory engagement) versus grandmother's "sentimentality" (ritual as transaction). A wrong answer missing "taste" or claiming gustatory is absent shows the student skims instead of annotates, a fatal error in board exam close-reading questions.

questions.q: Compare the visual imagery of the mali's "horrifying and revengeful" face (childhood) with the visual imagery of the newspaper woman's "bold streak of white in her short hair" (Duvidha). How do these two images function as visual metaphors for the author's evolving relationship with authority?
questions.a: The mali's face = oppressive, arbitrary authority that punishes curiosity (childhood fear). The newspaper woman = liberated, self-defined authority that commands attention (artistic vision). The first is imposed from outside (politician's gardener); the second is constructed from within (choreographer's creation). The contrast traces Lakhia's journey from suppressed subject to author of her own image. A wrong answer describing only physical features ("one is angry, one has white hair") without linking to authority/agency fails the analytical demand of Class 11 appreciation questions.

questions.q: Evaluate which metaphor more organically arises from Lakhia's identity as a dancer-choreographer: "life as a patchwork" (para 1) or "life as pre-recorded cassettes" (later). Justify with two specific connections to dance practice.
questions.a: "Patchwork" is more organic. Connection 1: Choreography assembles discrete movements (patches) into a coherent design (quilt) – exactly "bridges between life experiences and work in dance". Connection 2: Patchwork requires "perfecting technique" (cutting, stitching) before "throwing it overboard" (improvising within structure) – mirroring Ram Gopal's advice. "Cassettes" implies fixed, replayable recording – antithetical to live dance's ephemeral, responsive nature. A wrong answer choosing "cassettes" because "it's modern" ignores the author's explicit artistic philosophy and the text's emphasis on craft/process.

questions.q: Compose a 6-line free verse poem about a personal "crossroads" moment using: (a) at least three distinct imagery types, (b) one original metaphor, (c) no clichés ("fork in road", "light at tunnel end"). Title it "Atah Kim" (What now?).
questions.a:
*Atah Kim*  
Cold chai film on steel rim (gustatory/tactile)  
Monsoon drums on asbestos roof (auditory)  
My shadow detaches from the wall (visual)  
Fear is a landlord changing locks (metaphor)  
Keys I never owned turn to dust (tactile/visual)  
The door was never locked – I am the hinge (metaphor/resolution)  
A poor answer uses only visual imagery, relies on similes ("like a crossroads"), or copies the prompt's language – showing failure to internalize the essay's demand for multi-sensory, metaphorical thinking.
